5.26.m: Śeṣa said: / Śatrughna, seeing that army of dreadful appearance like a cloud, / surrounded by numerous elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers,
spoke these words in a deep voice to Sumati, / attended by learned men versed in the analysis of diverse speeches:
Śatrughna said: / 'O Sumati, whose city has this excellent sacrificial horse reached? / I behold this army surging like the waves of the milk ocean.
Whose is this furious army, equipped with four divisions, / that shines before us, drawn up with resolve for battle?
Explain all this to me truly as I ask, / knowing which I shall direct my soldiers to their battle stations.'
Hearing these words, Sumati of noble intellect, / pleased, spoke these words to Śatrughna, scorcher of foes:
Sumati said: / 'O King, nearby lies the auspicious city named Cakrāṅkā, / wherein people are freed from sin through devotion to Viṣṇu.
The lord of that city is this Subāhu, foremost of those who know dharma; / he shines here before you, surrounded by sons and grandsons.
Ever devoted to his own wife, averse to the wives of others, / the narration of Viṣṇu remains in his ears, revealing no other purpose.
The king takes no property of another beyond his one-sixth share; / brāhmaṇas are worshipped by that righteous one solely through devotion to Viṣṇu.
Constantly delighting in service, he is a bee at the lotus feet of Viṣṇu; / he is devoted to his own dharma, and turned away from the dharma of others.
Indeed, no warrior's strength anywhere equals his; / hearing of his son's fall, he is overcome with anger and grief.
Equipped with the four divisions, he has come forward for battle. / Yet you too have many warriors, led by Lakṣmīnidhi;
they will conquer them with hosts of weapons; order them at once, for they seek your welfare.' / Having heard his words, Śatrughna spoke to his foremost warriors,
whose minds were filled with a flood of martial delight born of reaching the battlefield: / 'Today a heron-shaped battle formation has been arranged by Subāhu’s surrounding soldiers.
Which master of weapons will pierce those warriors standing at its beak and wings? / Let the hero who has the power to pierce it and is intent upon victory
take the betel roll from my lotus hand!' / Then the heroic Lakṣmīnidhi accepted it to pierce the heron formation.
Knowing all weapons and divine missiles, surrounded by many heroes, / he spoke these words: 'O King, I shall go to break the heron formation!'
Formerly Bhārgava was the breaker of the Krauñca mountain, and so shall I be.' / Then [Śatrughna] spoke to another hero: 'Who will go with him?'
Then Puṣkala resolved to follow behind him, / as did Riputāpa, Nīlaratna, Ugrāśva, and Vīramardana.
By Śatrughna’s command they all set out to break that heron formation; / and Śatrughna too, mounted on his chariot and bearing all superior weapons,
marched behind him, surrounded by many soldiers. / Then the two oceans of rival armies were seen advancing,
swelling with great waves, as if prepared to bring about the destruction of the world. / Then loud war-drums were struck in both armies;
battle drums and the sounds of conches were heard on every side, / horses neighed there, and elephants trumpeted loudly.
Foremost warriors shouted war-cries, chariot wheel-rims roared; / furious heroes there, proud of the strength of Subāhu,
were seen in large numbers in the battle, shouting, 'Cut them down! Cleave them!' / While the armies of Śatrughna and his enemy were thus prepared for battle,
Lakṣmīnidhi spoke to that Suketu stationed at the beak. / Lakṣmīnidhi said: / 'Know me as the son of Janaka, named Lakṣmīnidhi,
skilled in all weapons and missiles, adept in every mode of combat. / Release the horse of Rāmacandra, who has bitten down on all demons;
otherwise, pierced by my arrows, you will go to the abode of Yama!' / To that foremost warrior who spoke thus, Suketu, swiftly hastening,
strung his bow quickly and stood firm, discharging arrows. / Those arrows with sharp nodes and golden feathers, spreading on all sides,
and discharged six sharp arrows adorned with keen nodes / upon his chest.
Those arrows, tearing open the heart of Subhuja's brother, / passed through and were seen on the ground, stained and filthy with blood.
His heart pierced by those arrows, Suketu, filled with rage, / struck back with twenty sharp arrows of bent nodes.
Both their limbs pierced with arrows, both drenched in blood, / they were seen by the soldiers like two flowering kiṃśuka trees.
Releasing tens of millions of arrows and fitting shafts with swiftness, / the two of mighty strength could not be discerned by anyone, so quick were their hands.
Drawing their fine bows into circles, raining streams of arrows, / they were like two fresh clouds in the sky obeying Indra’s command.
Their arrows were seen only as they decapitated elephants, horses, / foot-soldiers, and heroes—not when they were fitted or released.
The earth was filled with noble warriors wearing diadems and earrings, / bows and arrows in hand, their lower lips bitten in fury.
As the two fought with pride, both knowing all weapons and missiles, / a terrible, great battle took place that astonished the gods.
A tremendous clash occurred, tearing through ten million warriors; / no one anywhere could see the sky through the mesh of arrows.
At that moment, the heroic Lakṣmīnidhi, crusher of foes, / fitted eight firm, sharpened arrows onto his bow.
With four the hero brought Suketu’s horses to destruction; / with one, laughing, he swiftly cut down his dread banner.
With one he felled the charioteer’s head from his body to the ground; / filled with wrath, with one he cut his bow along with its string.
With one the swift king pierced Suketu in the heart. / Beholding that wondrous deed, the warriors were filled with astonishment.
His bow cut, deprived of his chariot, his horses killed, his charioteer slain, / seizing a massive mace, he advanced, eager to fight.
Perceiving him coming, skilled in mace-fighting / and equipped with a great mace, [Lakṣmīnidhi] descended from his chariot,
taking up a great mace forged entirely of iron, / its parts adorned with gold, endowed with all manner of splendor.
Lakṣmīnidhi, exceedingly enraged, hurrying to Suketu's chest, / struck his heart with a mace resembling the fire of a thunderbolt.
Struck by the mace, the hero did not tremble, O great sage, / like an elephant in rut struck with garlands by a boy.
That foremost of heroes then said to King Lakṣmīnidhi: / “Endure one blow of mine, if you are a hero, O scorcher of foes!”
Having spoken thus, he struck [him] severely on the forehead with a mace; / struck on the brow by the mace, vomiting blood, he became exceedingly enraged.
he struck him on the head with a mace that was death incarnate; / Suketu also, knower of dharma, struck him on the shoulder.
Thus exceedingly enraged, skilled in mace-fighting, / waging a mace duel, each desiring victory over the other,
confounded by mutual blows, intent on killing each other, / neither gave way nor was either defeated in the battle.
On the crown of the head, on the forehead, likewise on the shoulder, in the heart, and all over their limbs, / the two warriors of great strength and valor were drenched with torrents of blood.
Then the mighty, swift Lakṣmīnidhi, enraged, raised his mace / and went to strike the powerful younger brother of the king upon the heart.
Seeing him approaching, bearing his own great mace, / the king's brother went swiftly to kill him by force, strength matching strength.
The mace hurled by him, this [warrior] caught in his own hand; / with that very mace, the mighty one struck him in the heart.
King Lakṣmīnidhi, seeing his own mace taken away by him, / desired to fight that most powerful one in hand-to-hand combat.
Then the king's younger brother, enraged, seized him with his arms; / the best among heroes fought, being an expert in all types of combat.
Then Lakṣmīnidhi struck him in the heart with his fist; / then he too, raising his fist, struck him on the head.
With fists resembling thunderbolts and fierce slaps of the palm, / biting their lower lip-sprouts, the two enraged men struck each other.
Fist against fist, teeth against teeth, hair-pulling, nail against nail, / between the two there was a tumultuous combat that made the hair stand on end.
Then the enraged brother of the king, seizing the king by the foot / and whirling him around, cast him down to the ground.
Lakṣmīnidhi, grasping that younger brother of the king by the hand / and whirling him around a hundred times on high, slammed him upon an elephant's lap.
He, fallen then to the ground, having regained consciousness a moment later, / likewise whirled [Lakṣmīnidhi] with speed in the sky, full of valor.
Thus fighting, the two again engaged in hand-to-hand combat, / foot against foot, hand against hand, chest to chest, face to face.
Thus locked together, desiring to kill each other, / both indeed overcome by exhaustion, both indeed fainted.
Seeing that, filled with wonder, thousands praised them: / “Blessed is King Lakṣmīnidhi! Blessed is the mighty younger brother of the king!”

5.27.m: Śeṣa said: / Citrāṅga, seated on the neck of a krauñca-bird [chariot], standing in his chariot, adorned by warriors, / plunged into that army as the Boar [plunged] into the ocean.
Stringing his very firm bow that sounded like the roar of a raincloud, / he released sharp arrows that burned millions of enemies.
With all their limbs pierced by his arrows, excellent warriors lay down [dead] in great numbers, / with their diadems and armor, biting their lips.
When the battle had thus begun, Puṣkala went forth to fight, / taking his bow decorated with gems, the scorcher of enemies.
The appearance of those two who met was exceedingly captivating, / like that of Skanda and Tāraka in the ancient battle of Tāraka.
Drawing his bow quickly, ambidextrous Puṣkala / swiftly struck him with straight-jointed arrows.
Citrāṅga also, overcome with rage, holding aloft arrows with his bow, / released them repeatedly over the battlefield.
Neither the taking [of arrows], nor the aiming, nor the releasing / was seen; only the two of them were seen with their bows bent into circles.
Then Puṣkala, enraged, pierced that eminent great warrior / in the chest with a hundred arrows.
Citrāṅga cut all those arrows into sesamum-sized bits in an instant, / and struck Puṣkala on his limbs with sharp arrows.
With a splendid whirlwind-missile, Puṣkala whirled his divine chariot / in the sky; that became like a marvel.
Having spun for merely a muhūrta, that chariot with its horses, / held fast, regained its position on the battlefield with difficulty.
Seeing his valor, Citrāṅga, exceedingly enraged, / wise and skilled in all missiles, said to Puṣkala:
Citrāṅga said: / “A deed well done by you, approved by noble warriors in battle: / my chariot along with its horses was spun in the sky for a moment.
Now behold my valor also, proclaimed by noble warriors! / You shall wander through the sky and be honored by the immortals!”
Having spoken thus, he, knowing the highest missiles and foremost knower of all dharma, / released an exceedingly terrible missile with his bow in battle.
Pierced by that arrow, [Puṣkala] whirled in the sky like a bird in the battle, / with his chariot, with his horses, with his banner, and with his charioteer.
Having spun with great speed in the sky, that best of chariots, / before it could regain stability, another arrow was released [at it].
Again the chariot spun around along with the charioteer; / witnessing that deed of his, the king's son felt great wonder.
Somehow Puṣkala, slayer of enemy heroes, regained his footing, / and struck down his chariot with arrows, along with its charioteer and horses.
His chariot broken, the hero resorted to another; / that one also was quickly shattered by Puṣkala with arrows on the battleground.
Mounting yet another, as soon as he came forward, / he smashed his chariot again with sharp arrows.
Thus ten chariots of the king's son were shattered / by the heroic Puṣkala, who shone in the great conflict.
Then Citrāṅga, standing in a decorated chariot in battle, / came with speed to fight against Puṣkala in the conflict.
He struck Puṣkala with five arrows in the battle; / exceedingly struck by those arrows, the son of Bharata was pained.
Enraged, raising his bow, the great warrior released / ten sharp arrows beautifully adorned with golden feathers into his chest.
Those most terrible arrows drank his blood; / having drunk, they fell to the ground like the ancestors of false witnesses.
Then Citrāṅga, enraged, took up five broad-headed arrows / and discharged them at the forehead of the glorious son of Bharata.
Struck by those broad-headed arrows, enraged, holding an arrow / on his excellent bow, he made a vow regarding Citrāṅga's destruction:
“Hear, O hero, my prompt vow concerning your death! / Knowing it, you must fight with alertness here!
If with this arrow I do not deprive you of life, / then whatever world is attained by people subject to Yama
for violating a chaste woman who is adorned with good character and conduct, / let that world indeed be mine! My promise is true!”
Hearing these excellent words, the slayer of enemy heroes laughed; / the wise hero spoke auspicious words to Puṣkala:
"Death indeed must come to living beings everywhere and always; / therefore I have no sorrow in dying, O crest-jewel of heroes!
The vow made by you, heroic one, endowed with heroism, / is indeed true. Now listen further to the great declaration uttered by me:
If I do not split your arrow that is set on killing me, / then hear the vow of me, who pride myself as a hero of all heroes!
Whoever causes an inner breakdown for one wishing to go to a pilgrimage site, / or considers any other vow higher than the Ekādaśī vow—
let that person's sin be mine alone if I fail my vow!" / Having spoken this word, he became silent and took up his bow.
Then, drawing an excellent arrow from his quiver, / he [Puṣkala] uttered clear words that bring death to enemies.
Puṣkala said: / "If I have worshipped Rāma's two feet with an guileless heart, / then may my word prove true!
If, having enjoyed my own wife, I acknowledge no other woman in my mind, / by that truth let my word come true in battle!"
Having uttered these words, he quickly discharged an arrow fitted to his bow, / resembling the fire of cosmic dissolution, which severed the hero's head.
Seeing that loosed arrow, that powerful prince / placed on his bow a sharp arrow resembling the fire of cosmic dissolution.
By that arrow, the arrow bent on his death was split in two; / a great cry of grief arose when that shaft was shattered.
The rear half fell to the ground; the front half, equipped with the arrow-head, / swiftly severed his neck in an instant, like the stalk of a lotus.
Then, seeing him falling to the ground, his soldiers, / crying out in great grief, all took to flight.
That splendid head on the earth, with its diadem and earrings, / shone brilliantly fallen there, like the lunar orb fallen from the sky.
Seeing him fallen, the heroic Puṣkala, son of Bharata, / plunged into that battle array, adorned solely by all the heroes.

5.28.m: Śeṣa said: / Then, beholding his haughty son fallen and lifeless, / the king lamented bitterly, afflicted with sorrow over his son.
He struck his head with both hands, deeply grieved, / trembling violently and shedding tears from his lotus-eyes.
Taking up the fallen face, charming like the lunar orb, / drenched with blood from wounds made by Puṣkala's arrows and adorned with earrings,

with splendid curved eyebrows and bitten lower lip, / kissing his lotus-face, he said this while lamenting:

"Alas, heroic son! Why do you not look upon me, whose heart is anxious, / with your pair of bright eyes, O hero?"
Why are you devoid of speech that delights me, / and appear with a mind submerged in an ocean of anger?
Tell me, son, why do you not address me again, smiling, / and delight me, my dear son, with nectar-like sweet tastes?
Take Śatrughna's horse, adorned with white fly-whisks / and resplendent with gold leaf; abandon sleep, O wise one!
Here stands Puṣkala before us, radiant with prowess, foremost in majesty, scorcher of foes, / wielding his bow, the slayer of enemy heroes.
Fend him off with sharp arrows released from your bow! / Why do you lie bewildered, O hero, in the midst of battle?
Elephants, foot soldiers, and chariot riders, afflicted with fear, / are coming to you for refuge; look upon them, O wise one!
Son, without you, how can I endure on the battlefield / the sharp arrows of Śatrughna loosed from his fierce bow?
Therefore, when I am bereft of you, who can protect me? / If you abandon sleep, then I will be capable of victory."
Lamenting thus bitterly, the king struck his own chest / repeatedly with his hand, tormented by sorrow over his son.
Then Vicitra and Damana, standing in their respective chariots, / bowed at their father's feet and spoke words fitting the occasion:
"O king, while we live, what sorrow is in your heart? Tell us! / Death in battle is regarded as great and desirable for heroes.
O, fortunate is this Citrāṅga, who shines on the field of heroes, / wearing his diadem, biting both his lips, our lord!
Tell us quickly: what desired task shall the two of us accomplish for you this very day? / We two will destroy the entire army of Śatrughna and leave it without a master!
This very day in battle we shall fell Puṣkala, the slayer of our brother, / from his chariot, severing his head adorned with a diadem.
Cast off grief! Why do you appear so afflicted with sorrow, O wise one? / Command the two of us, worthy of honor, and turn your mind likewise to battle!"
Hearing these words of the two sons who considered themselves heroes, / the great king cast off his sorrow and set his mind on fighting.
Those two as well, wild with battle-fury and desiring an opponent, / advanced into the enemy's camp, which was crowded with countless warriors.
Damana fought with Riputāpa, and the other [Vicitra] with Nīlaratna; / the two heroes fought in battle like two rain-clouds in the monsoon season.
The king, standing on a gold-plated chariot varied with gems, / richly adorned with a bejeweled pole, wielding a bow, mighty,
went out to fight Śatrughna, who was surrounded by crores of heroes, / treating as grass the great heroes skilled in the science of archery.
Seeing Subāhu approaching to fight, filled with fury, / and, on account of his son's destruction, causing the slaughter of his whole army and more,
Hanūmān, moving at Śatrughna's side, rushed at him, / using his claws as weapons and roaring loudly like a cloud in battle.
Subāhu, laughing, spoke these words to Hanūmān, / who was approaching with a great roar, his eyes filled with wrath:
"Where has Puṣkala gone after slaying my son on the field of battle? / This very day I shall quickly bring down his head with its gleaming earrings!
Where is Śatrughna, guardian of the horse? Where is Rāma? Where are the warriors? / Let them behold me in battle approaching as the destroyer of life!"
Hearing those words of his, Hanūmat said to him: / "Śatrughna, slayer of Lavaṇa, stands as protector of the army."
How could he fight in battle, O king, while his servant stands before him? / Having conquered me in battle, O bull among men, you may proceed to him."
As he spoke thus, he swiftly pierced that very fierce monkey / in the heart with ten arrows, as he stood like a mountain peak.
Catching those incoming sharp arrows that tear through enemies / in his cupped hands, he crushed them into sesame-sized pieces.
Having crushed those arrows, roaring with deep thunderings, / the mighty one wrapped [Subāhu's] chariot in his tail and lifted it high into the air.
Then, situated right there in the sky, that best of kings / struck the tail repeatedly with his sharp-pointed arrows.
Struck at the tip of his tail by arrows with sunken joints, / he released that celestial chariot adorned with gold.
Released swiftly by him, with eyes filled with fury, / he struck Hanūmān, the best of monkeys, with sharp arrows.
Hanūmān, pierced by arrows and drenched with blood everywhere, / the lord of monkeys, conceived a great wrath toward the king.
Seizing with his teeth that chariot along with its horses, / he swiftly crushed it to powder; that was wondrous indeed.
Seeing his chariot being shattered, the powerful king hastened, / mounted another chariot, and fought that mighty one.
On the tail, face, chest, arm, and two feet, the king, / skilled in aiming arrows and knowing supreme weapons, struck him.
Then the enraged, best of monkeys, leaping swiftly, / struck with his foot upon the chest of the king who shone among good warriors.
Struck by his foot, he fell to the ground unconscious, / vomiting hot blood from his mouth, trembling with gasps of breath.
Then Hanūmān, greatly enraged on the field of battle, / swiftly crushed the horses, the heroes, and the elephants as well.
Then his brother Suketu and King Lakṣmīnidhi, / both well-armored, stepped forward for battle.
Seeing the king swooned, the men fled away, / wounded here and there by multitudes of arrows showered by Puṣkala.
Seeing his army being shattered, the king's powerful son / Damana checked it, like a dam holding back the surging sea.
Then the king, swooning, saw a dream indeed / in the midst of battle, struck down by the blow of the monkey's forefoot:
Rāmacandra was in Ayodhyā in a pavilion on the bank of the Sarayū, / surrounded by many Brahmins, the best of sacrificers;
there were gods headed by Brahmā, there were tens of millions of universes, / praising him repeatedly with hymns with folded palms;
Nārada and others, with vīṇās shining in their hands, were singing / of Rāma, dark-complexioned, with beautiful eyes, holding the horn of a deer;
apsarases danced there, Ghṛtācī, Menakā, and others; / the Vedas, assuming embodied forms, attended upon Rāghava;
and whatever variety of things existed, endowed with every beauty, / [he was] the giver of all that, bestowing enjoyment upon devotees.
Seeing these and other things, he regained his waking consciousness, / his mind stricken by the brāhmaṇa's curse, crying: "What did I see?"
Rising, he set out on foot toward the feet of Śatrughna, / accompanied by ten million servants and surrounded by ten million chariots.
Summoning Suketu, Vicitra, and also Damana / as they prepared to fight, he who knew dharma restrained them.
The great king, righteous-souled and united with dharma, said to them: / "O brother, O two sons, listen to my words endowed with dharma.
Do not fight anymore quickly! A great injustice has occurred, / since Damana captured the mighty steed of Rāmacandra.
This Rāma is the supreme Brahman, beyond cause and effect, / the lord of the moving and unmoving universe, having assumed a human body.
Indeed, I have now realized this supreme knowledge of Brahman, / having formerly had my wealth of knowledge stolen by Asitāṅga's curse, O sinless ones!
Formerly, I went on a pilgrimage to sacred sites desiring to know the truth; / there I saw many sages who best knew dharma.
With a desire to know, I approached the sage Asitāṅga; / then the Brahmin, taking compassion upon me, spoke:
'He who is the lord of Ayodhyā is designated the supreme Brahman; / his queen Jānakī is remembered as pure consciousness in visible form.
Yogins worship him directly through self-restraint and the rest, / desiring to cross over the impassable, boundless ocean of saṃsāra.
By merely being remembered, he who has Garuḍa on his banner removes great sins; / the wise one who serves him shall cross over saṃsāra.'
Then I laughed at the Brahmin: 'Who is this Rāma, a mere human? / Who is this Queen Jānakī, afflicted with joy and sorrow?
How can the unborn be born? What is the deed of the non-doer here? / Speak to me, O sage, of what is beyond birth, sorrow, and old age!'
"When I spoke thus, that lord among sages became angry and cursed me: / 'Without understanding His true nature, you talk back to me, vile one!'"
You revile this Rāma, laughing that he is a human; / therefore, deluded regarding the truth, you will become a glutton living only for your belly.'
Then, filled with pity, I grasped his feet; / seeing my humility, that treasury of compassion spoke to me:
'When, O king, you create an obstacle to Rāma's sacrifice, / then Hanūmān will swiftly strike you with his foot.
Then, O king, you will know; not otherwise through your own intellect.' / Thus was I told formerly by him, and that has now been seen by me.
When the enraged Hanumān struck me in the chest, / then I saw the Lord of Ramā, the embodiment of the complete Brahman.
Therefore, O mighty ones, bring forth the splendid horse! / I surrender treasures, garments, and this kingdom.
Having seen Rāma in the merit-bestowing sacrifice, I will have achieved my purpose; / let them bring the horse to me; its surrender pleases me."

5.29.m: Śeṣa said: / Hearing their father's words, those fighters were delighted, / and said "So be it" to the great king, who was longing for a sight of Rāma.
The sons said: / "O king, we know no other than your lotus feet; / whatever has arisen from your heart, let that take place swiftly today.
Let the horse be brought there, adorned with white fly-whisks, / endowed with extreme splendor by garlands of gems, and smeared with sandalwood and the like.
The kingdom bears the fruit of your command, O master; the treasuries are full of abundant wealth; / the garments are very precious, fine, and of excellent quality;
sandalwood and camphor, very charming steeds, / elephants excited with rut, and chariots with golden yokes;
adorned with various ornaments of variegated colors and the like; / a hundred thousand maidservants and charming manservants;
gems resembling the sun and various kinds of jewels; / bright pearls born from the frontal lobes of elephants;
hundreds of thousands of corals, and whatever object is of great worth— / give all that to Rāmacandra, O wise king!
Surrender us sons, all our servants, O lord of the earth; / why do you not place the royal throne under his sway, O king?"
Śeṣa said: / Hearing the words of his sons, the lord of the earth became delighted, / and spoke to his heroic sons who were ready to carry out his words.
The king said: / "Let all of you, armored with weapons in hand / and accompanied by various chariots, bring the horse; then I shall go to the king."
Śeṣa said: / Hearing the king's words, Vicitra, Damana, / and Suketu, heroes in battle, went at his command, eager.
Having gone to the city, those heroes [brought] the very charming horse, / provided with white fly-whisks, decorated with gold plates and the like,
richly adorned with gem garlands, beautified with variegated patterns, / rich with decorations of various jewels, and well adorned with pearl nets.
Held by ropes by great heroes, soldiers in front and behind, / equipped with great weapons and missiles, endowed with every splendor,
a white parasol gleamed high above the horse's head, / while two fine chowries were waved repeatedly before him.
Perfumed with incenses like black agallochum, swift as the wind, / they led the horse of the sacrificial rite, the horse sacrifice, before the king.
Seeing that horse brought forward, adorned with pearl necklaces, / swift as thought and changing form at will, the wise king rejoiced.
Adorned with royal insignias and other ornaments, the exceedingly righteous king / went on foot to Śatrughna, accompanied by his sons and grandsons.
He went to make proper use of riches, which are ever fleeting, / knowing this [wealth] to be perishable and a source of grief for attached minds.
Then he saw Śatrughna, graced by a white umbrella, / and fanned with chowries by servants standing in front,
inquiring of Sumati about the story of Rāmacandra, / free from all word of fear, adorned with the splendor of a hero,
thronged by tens of millions of warriors eager to guard the horse, / and surrounded on all sides by thousands of monkeys.
Seeing Śatrughna's feet, he prostrated himself along with his son; / overjoyed, his mind fixed solely on Rāma, he said, “Blessed am I!”
Seeing that affectionate and formidable king, / Śatrughna arose from his seat and embraced him with both arms before all the warriors.
Having deeply honored that Śatrughna, the king, slayer of enemy heroes, / filled with joy, spoke in a choked voice:
Subāhu said: / “Today I am blessed, together with my sons, family, and mounts, / since I behold your feet, praised by tens of millions of kings.
By my foolish son this best of horses was seized; / forgive his improper conduct, O ocean of compassion!
He does not know the crest-jewel of the Raghus, the supreme deity of all the gods, / who effortlessly creates, destroys, and protects the universe.
This kingdom with all its limbs thriving, with abundant armies and mounts, / these treasuries filled with wealth, these sons, and we ourselves—
we all have Rāma as our master and are observers of your command. / Take it all to good effect; I have no contrary thought whatsoever.
Where is that Hanūmān, the black bee at the lotus feet of Rāma, / by whose favor I shall obtain the sight of the king of kings?
What is not obtained on this earth in the company of the virtuous, / by whose favor I, though foolish, crossed beyond the curse of a brahmin?
Having seen the great king today, whose eyes resemble lotus petals, / I shall obtain all the fruit of this birth, so difficult to attain in this world.
Indeed, much of my lifespan has passed in separation from Rāma; / very little remains. How then shall I behold the best of the Raghus?
Show me that Rāma, skillful in sacrificial acts, / by the dust of whose feet the sage’s beloved wife, turned to stone, was purified;
by the touch of whose arrow a bird, a crow, attained the supreme state; / and beholding whose lotus face in battle many have reached that state!
Those who take the name of this Lord of the Raghus with reverence / go to the supreme abode which is contemplated by yogins.
Blessed are the people living in Ayodhyā, who, drinking in / the lotus face of Rāma with the cups of their eyes, attain great prosperity and happiness!”
Having thus addressed the king and surrendered his mount, kingdom, and wealth, / he said: "I am your servant, O king of the earth!"
Hearing these words of the king, the conqueror of enemy cities, / eloquent and skilled in speech, answered that king:
Śatrughna said: / “Why do you speak thus, O king? You are an elder, revered by me. / All is yours; let this Damana govern your kingdom.
This is the duty of kṣatriyas: to wage battle. / Let all this kingdom and wealth return [to you] by my command.
Just as the Lord of the Raghus is always to be worshiped by me in speech and mind, / so you too, O protector of the earth, shall be honored by me.
Be prepared today to follow the horse, / equipped, armored, sword in hand, along with elephants, horses, and chariots.”
Hearing these words of Śatrughna, the king, / having anointed his son in the kingdom and being greatly honoured by Śatrughna,
surrounded by great chariot-warriors, performing the funeral rites according to rule / for his own son slain by Puṣkala on the field of battle,
grieved for a moment, being a knower of the truth, out of worldly perspective; / but that great chariot-warrior dispelled his grief with knowledge, remembering the Lord of the Raghus.
Ready, mounted upon a chariot, surrounded by a vast army, / he came to Śatrughna, preceded by great chariot-warriors.
Seeing that the king had arrived accompanied by his whole army, / he made up his mind to set forth in guarding the excellent horse.
That horse, marked with a tablet on his forehead, was released by him; / wandering counter-clockwise, he traversed many eastern realms.
Everywhere prostration was made by the kings there, who were honored by great heroes; / none seized him in anger.
Some brought colorful garments, some their own vast kingdoms, / some wealth, some people, and bowed down to him.

5.30.m: Śeṣa said: / Then the horse, adorned with the tablet, reached Tejaḥpura, / where the truthful king protects his subjects with truth.
Then, surrounded by tens of millions, the younger brother of the Lord of the Raghus, / following the horse, went before that [city], a crusher of enemy cities.
Seeing that charming city, adorned with multicolored ramparts, / shining all around with golden jars,
resplendent on all sides with thousands of temples, / where the monasteries of ascetics shone, filled with renunciants,
where the great goddess [Gaṅgā], who rests on the head of the three-eyed god, flows, / crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, resorted to by hosts of sages,
and where the smoke arising from the agnihotra fires in every house of the brahmins / purifies those whose minds are steeped in sin, O dear one;
King Śatrughna, the tormentor of enemies, / his mind filled with joy and wonder upon seeing that city, said to Sumati:
Śatrughna said: / "O minister, tell me, whose city is this within range of my sight, / protected by righteousness, which brings delight to the mind?"
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this speech of King Śatrughna, / Sumati related everything just as it was, without haughtiness.
Sumati said: / “Listen attentively, O master, to the auspicious tales of the Vaiṣṇava, / by hearing which one is freed even from sin equal to the killing of a brahmin.
A living liberated soul lives here, a bee at the lotus feet of Rāma: / Satyavat, a knower of sacrifice and its limbs, a performer [of rites], and a great protector.
His father, renowned in the world as Ṛtaṃbhara, exceedingly righteous, / obtained him having propitiated the sacred cow with many vows.
The cow, being pleased, granted him a son adorned with many virtues, / truthful and full of great splendor; know him to be that best of kings.”

Śatrughna said:
Who was King Ṛtaṃbhara, and for what purpose was the worship of the cow performed?
How was his son obtained, a Vaiṣṇava devoted to Viṣṇu?

Tell all this story of the Vaiṣṇava,
which, when heard, removes the mountain of great sins of living beings.

Śeṣa said:
Having heard this meaningful statement of Śatrughna,
he clearly told the narrative of his birth.

Formerly, King Ṛtaṃbhara was childless.
He had many wives, but he did not obtain a son through them.

Then, eagerly seeking prosperity, he asked the sage named Jābāli,
who had arrived by chance, the cause for the birth of a son.

Ṛtaṃbhara said:
Master, tell me, who am childless, the advice that brings about the birth of a son,
by doing which an excellent child may be born to perpetuate my lineage.

Having learned your auspicious and decisive word, I shall perform it—
whether charity, a vow, [a visit to] a sacred bathing place, or a sacrifice, O best of sages.
Hearing the king's words, that best of sages spoke words / that would bring about the birth of a son to the bowed king who sought a son.

For one who desires to obtain offspring, O lord, there are three means:
the grace of Viṣṇu, or of a cow, or again of Śiva.

Therefore, O king, perform the worship of the cow whose body is divine,
in whose tail, mouth, horns, and back the gods are established.

She, being pleased, will swiftly grant the desired [object] endowed with dharma.
Knowing this, perform the worship of cows, O Ṛtaṃbhara.

Whoever constantly worships a cow in his house with grass and other things—
his gods and ancestors are indeed constantly satisfied.

Whoever observes an auspicious vow and provides daily food for a cow with restraint,
by that truth all his desires shall be fulfilled.

A thirsty cow tied in the house, a menstruating maiden in the house,
and a deity with faded flowers destroy merit previously accumulated.

A man who prevents a cow grazing on his own grass—
his ancestors tremble, on the verge of falling.

A mortal of deluded mind who strikes a cow with a stick
goes to the city of Dharmarāja, deprived of his hands.

His ancestors who have fallen into low states dance when someone wards off biting flies:
‘Our fortunate son will deliver us!’

On this very subject, they cite this ancient legendary history,
the wonderful past event of Janaka in the city of Dharmarāja.

Once, King Janaka abandoned his vital breaths through yoga;
then an aerial chariot arrived, decorated with a network of tiny bells.

Mounting it, the king departed, his body borne by attendants;
on the path, he went near Saṃyaminī, the city of Dharma.

Then, evildoers being tormented in millions of hells
attained ease on receiving the breeze from Janaka's body.

In hell, the torment born of burning became a source of comfort for them;
then the great suffering was destroyed by the breeze from Janaka's body.

Then, seeing him departing, the living beings afflicted by sin,
terrified and not desiring separation from him, cried out exceedingly.

They uttered a pitiful plea: ‘Do not go away from here, O virtuous one!
By the contact of the breeze from your body we become happy and free from torment.’
Having heard these words, the supremely righteous king, / filled with a flood of compassion, reflected in his mind.

‘If from me there should be happiness for creatures here, then again
I will remain right here in this city; this is my delightful heaven.’

Having resolved thus, the king stood right there before hell,
rendering happiness to creatures, his mind moved with compassion.

Then Dharma arrived at the grief-bestowing gate of hell,
causing intense torments to be inflicted on the perpetrators of various sins.

Then he saw King Janaka standing at the gate
in his aerial chariot, an agent of great merit endowed with compassion.

The lord of the dead said to Janaka with gentle speech:
‘O king, crown jewel of all righteousness, from where have you arrived?

This is a place for sinners, the wicked, and slayers of living beings.
Men like you, creators of merit, do not come [here], O king.

Those men come here who are intent on injuring others,
devoted to slandering others, and intent on [stealing] others' wealth.

Or a man who abandons a virtuous wife devoted to serving him
without any fault—that man arrives here.

A man who deceives a friend, enticed by greed for wealth,
comes here and receives severe torment from me.

The foolish-minded person who does not remember Rāma in mind, speech, or deed,
even through deceit, hatred, or mockery—

I bind him again, cast him into these [hells], and cook him.
Those by whom the lord of men was remembered have their hellish anguish warded off.

Sin remains in the limbs of human beings, O king, only so long
as the tongue does not utter "Rāma" on account of the evil mind in Kali.

Those who are perpetrators of great sins, O wise king,
my servants bring them here; they are incapable of even looking upon people like you.

Therefore, go, great king, and enjoy manifold pleasures;
mounting the excellent aerial chariot, enjoy the merit you have earned.’
Having heard these words of Dharmarāja, their lord, / filled with a flood of compassion, he spoke to Dharmarāja:

Janaka said:
‘I will not go, O lord, out of compassion for these souls.
Indeed, by the breeze from my body these [souls] staying here have found happiness.

If you release all these who are residing in hell, O king,
then, joyful, I will go to the heaven inhabited by virtuous people.’

Jābāli said:
Then, hearing this speech, he replied to Janaka,
pointing out one by one the many souls residing in hell.

Later, casting this guilty one into the wombs of swine,
he is to be brought down among humans marked with the sign of a eunuch.

By this one, another's wife was repeatedly embraced by force;
therefore, he is cooked here in Raurava for a hundred years.

This evil-minded one stole another's property and enjoyed it;
therefore, having cut off his hands, I shall cook him in pus and blood.

This one did not honor with words or welcome a guest
who arrived in the evening, afflicted with hunger.

Therefore, he is to be cast into Tāmisra, filled with firewood;
tormented by large black bees, let him suffer torment for a hundred years.

This one, indeed, unashamedly censured another loudly,
and this other one, turning his ears, listened to it repeatedly.

Therefore, these two have fallen into a blind well, afflicted with sorrow;
this betrayer of a friend, distressed, is severely cooked in Raurava.

Therefore, having made them experience the fruits of their sins, I shall release them.
Go, O tiger among men, creator of a heap of merit!’

Jābāli said:
When he had thus pointed out the souls who had committed sins, he became silent.
That devotee of Rāma, his eyes filled with compassion, said:

Janaka said:
‘How may there be liberation from hell for these suffering souls?
Tell that quickly, by doing which they may obtain happiness.’

If you would liberate even these committers of great sins,
then, O great king, surrender the merit about which I speak.

Once, rising early in the morning, with a mind of pure disposition,
that glorious lord of the Raghus, whose very name removes great sin, was meditated upon [by you],

and it was uttered by you with a pure mind: 'Rāma, Rāma!'
Surrender that merit to these, by which their release from hell may come about.

Jābāli said:
Having heard this speech of that wise Dharmarāja,
the great king gave the merit accumulated since his birth.

"By the merits performed since birth arising from the worship of the lord of the Raghus,
let there be delightful release from hell for these here!"

As he was speaking thus, the souls residing in hell
were instantly freed from hell and came to bear divine bodies.

They said to Janaka: "O king, by your grace we are instantly
freed from the sorrow-giving hell and shall go to the supreme abode."

Seeing those men emerging from hell, radiant as the sun,
he who was devoted to compassion for all living beings rejoiced greatly in his heart.

They all went to the world of heaven adorned by the gods,
praising Janaka, the great king, an ocean of compassion.

5.31.m:
Jābāli said:
Then, when those men who had been in hell had departed,
the king questioned Kīnāśa, the best among all knowers of dharma.

The king said:
O Dharmarāja, it was said by you that men who commit sins
come to your abode, and not those delighted in discourses on dharma.

By what sin did my arrival here take place, O righteous one?
Tell me truly all that cause of my sin from the beginning.
Having heard those words of his, O scorcher of foes, Dharmarāja / then recounted to him his arrival at the city of Yama in this manner.
Dharmarāja said: / O king, great is your merit; no one on earth possesses such [merit], / O bee [drinking] the nectar of the pair of feet of the lord of the Raghus!
The heavenly river of your fame purifies all sinners laden with impurities, / causing supreme delight and carrying the wicked across.

Even so, there remains a particle of sin in you, O best of kings,
by which you, though filled with merit, have come to the vicinity of Saṃyaminī.

Once indeed, through pride of power, you hindered a grazing cow;
by the ripening of that sin, the sight of the door of hell has occurred.

Now, freed from sin and endowed with great merit,
enjoy the vast and numerous pleasures earned by your own merits.

The ocean of compassion, the lord of the Raghus, wishing to bring happiness to these,
sent a Vaiṣṇava upon the great road to Saṃyaminī.

If you had not come by this path, O one of good vows,
how would their liberation from hell have taken place?

Those like you, distressed by the distress of others and abodes of compassion,
always bring an end to the distress of living beings, O wise one.

Jābāli said:
Bowing to Śamana who was speaking thus, he went to heaven
by means of a divine, splendid celestial vehicle adorned with a host of apsarases.

Therefore cows are to be worshipped continually; one should not revile them even with the mind;
reviling them, one goes to hell for as long as fourteen Indras rule.

Therefore, O best of kings, perform worship of the cow;
she, being pleased, will swiftly grant a son devoted to dharma.

Sumati said:
Having heard that, he questioned him respectfully about the worship of the cow:
"How is she to be worshipped with effort? What does she do for a man?"

Jābāli explained the worship of the cow according to the rule:
"Every day, one keeping the vow should go to the forest to graze the cow.

One should feed barley to the cow and then collect [the grains] from her dung;
those barley grains must be eaten by one desiring a son, O lord of the earth.

When she drinks water, then pure water should be drunk;
when she stands in an elevated place, then one should remain seated [only then].

One should continually ward off biting insects and gather fodder oneself;
to one who acts thus, she will grant a son intent on dharma."

Sumati said:
Having heard this speech, the virtuous Ṛtaṃbhara, desiring a son,
undertook the vow, performing the worship of the cow.

Every day he kept the cow satisfied with fodder and the like;
the wise king warded off biting insects, showing diligence in eating the barley.

As he was thus worshipping the cow, many days passed,
while she grazed on grass and other plants in the midst of the forest, free from fear.

Once the king, his gaze cast on beholding the beauty of that forest,
wandered about full of curiosity.

Then a lion, coming from the interior of the forest, struck the cow
who was lowing repeatedly and pitifully, distressed under the lion's weight.

Then the king, coming up and beholding his mother[-cow],
seeing her slain by the lion, wept, extremely agitated.

Grieved, he approached Jābāli, the best of sages,
and asked about expiation for that cow-killing caused by negligence.

What shall I do at your command for the expiation of that sin,
or how can there be the completion of my vow that grants a son?"
To that king who had spoken thus, the best of sages said: / "O protector of the earth, there exist means for removing this sin."

For the slayer of a brāhmaṇa, for the ungrateful, and for the drinker of liquor, O wise one,
expiations exist, and they remove all sins.

Through difficult penances, cāndrāyaṇa penances, gifts, vows, with observances and restraints,
sins undergo dissolution for one who observes them according to rule.

Yet for two committers of a heap of sins there is no expiation:
for one who kills a cow intentionally, and for one who reviles Nārāyaṇa.

The lowest of men who even in his mind desires harm to cows
goes to the place of hell for as long as fourteen Indras rule.

The unfortunate man who should revile the god Hari even once
shall also see hell surrounded by his sons and grandsons.

Therefore, knowingly reviling Hari or inflicting suffering upon cows,
one never attains liberation from hell, O lord of men.

However, for cow-killing incurred through ignorance there is indeed an expiation:
go to the wise devotee of Rāma, Ṛtuparṇa.

He indeed looks upon all enemies and friends with equal vision;
he will quickly tell you the expiation for this cow-killing.

Though you formerly invaded his lands and were exiled by him,
renounce all enmity and go to Ṛtuparṇa.

Whatever he shall say, perform that quickly with concentrated mind,
so that the expiation for the sin committed by you will indeed be accomplished."

Having heard his words, he went to Ṛtuparṇa,
the devotee of Rāma, upright and of equal vision towards foe and friend.

He related to him what had happened, beginning with the killing of the cow;
and he too reflected upon a means for the expiation of that sin.

Then, having reflected for a moment, the wise King Ṛtuparṇa, knowledgeable in dharma,
smiled and addressed these words to Ṛtambhara:

"Who am I, O King, in the presence of sages who know the scriptures?
Having bypassed them, why have you come to me, a fool who merely considers himself learned?

If you have faith in me, then I shall speak a little.
Listen respectfully, O tiger among men, to what I say.

Worship the venerable Lord of the Raghus in deed, mind, and speech;
without deceit, please the Lord of the worlds, O noble-minded one.

When pleased, he will grant you every wish residing in your heart;
he will destroy the sin of the killing of the cow committed in ignorance.

Remembering Rāma, O righteous one, care for the cow, O best of men;
giving gold to a twice-born, you will obtain expiation for your sin."

Sumati said:
Having heard that statement, King Ṛtambhara then,
recalling Rāma and with a purified mind, observed the vow.

Caring for the cow as before, he went to the great forest,
constantly remembering the name of Rāma and devoted to the welfare of all beings.

Pleased with him, Surabhi, being thoroughly gratified, said:
'O King, choose a boon from me, the wish residing in your heart.'

Then the king said: 'Give me a charming son
who is a devotee of Rāma, devoted to his father, and an observer of his own duty.'

Having granted the boon to that king desiring a son, the pleased,
compassionate divine wishing cow, Surabhi, vanished from sight.

In due course, he obtained a Vaiṣṇava son, a servant of Rāma;
then his father endowed him with the name Satyavat.

Having obtained the son Satyavat, supreme in devotion to his father
and of prowess equal to Indra, the great [king] attained the highest joy.

Having obtained a virtuous son, that king, filled with joy,
entrusted the great kingdom to him and went to the forest for austerities.

There, having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa with a mind filled with devotion,
the king, having shaken off all sin, went with his body to the abode of Hari.

5.32.m:
Sumati said:
That gentle king, renowned by the name Satyavān,
pleased the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of the Raghus, by his own duty.

Pleased with him, the Lord of Ramā granted unswerving devotion
at his own lotus feet—devotion difficult to obtain even through ten million merits—to the worshipper.

Untiring, full of compassion, he continually recites
the story of the venerable Lord of the Raghus, which purifies all worlds.

He who does not worship the god, the Lord of the Raghus, the husband of Ramā,
is struck by him with punishments that inspire fear even in Yama.

From eight years of age until eighty years,
up to that age the Ekādaśī vow was caused to be observed by all men through him.

Whose beloved is the tulasī, and whose neck is never left
by the excellent garland from the lotus feet of the Lord of Ramā.

He is worthy of worship even by ṛṣis; how could he not be so by others?
He delights in the remembrance of the Lord of the Raghus, his sins shaken off and misfortunes destroyed.

Having recognized this most wondrous horse of Rāmacandra,
he will come and deliver this kingdom, free from all troubles, to you.

What was asked by you, O King, has been told to you in full excellence.
What else do you ask, O master? Command me, and I shall do it."

Śeṣa said:
The horse, endowed with various wonders, went near that city.
Seeing it, all the citizens went and reported to the king.

The citizens said:
"A certain horse, white in color like the waters of the Gaṅgā,
shining with a golden tablet on its forehead, has arrived."

Having heard those charming words, pleasing to the heart, spoken by the people,
the king smiled and replied to them: "Let it be found out whose horse it is."

And they told him: "The horse, guarded by Śatrughna,
belonging to the lord of the earth, Rāma, is coming from within the city."

Having heard the two-syllabled, thoroughly charming name of Rāma,
he rejoiced exceedingly in his heart, marked by a choked voice.

"That Rāma, the lord of Ayodhyā, who is continually meditated upon by me in my heart—
his horse, along with Śatrughna, has arrived in my city!

Hanūmat, the servant of Rāma's feet, will be there—
he who never forgets Rāma in his mind at any time.

I shall go where Śatrughna is, where the son of the wind is,
and where other men, servants of Rāma's lotus feet, are."

Then he instructed his minister: "Taking all the great royal wealth,
come with me in all haste.

I shall go to protect the excellent horse of the Lord of the Raghus,
and to render the most rare service to Rāma's lotus feet."
Having spoken thus, he then marched forth toward Śatrughna with his soldiers; / meanwhile, Rāma's brother arrived at the city with his army.

Mighty warriors roared, chariots rumbled loudly,
and sounds of conches of victory and the sounds of flutes were everywhere.

Approaching with his ministers, King Satyavān
bowed at his feet and gave him the kingdom with its great wealth.

Śatrughna, knowing that king to be devoted to Rāma,
gave that great kingdom to his son, named Rukma.

Embracing Hanūmat, Subāhu the servant of Rāma,
and embracing the other devotees of Rāma, the highly renowned [king],

endowed with truth, regarded himself as having fulfilled his purpose;
he then rejoiced in his heart in the company of Śatrughna.

Meanwhile, the horse, well protected by warriors, went far ahead;
Śatrughna, accompanied by that king and surrounded by warriors, followed it.

5.33.m:
Śeṣa said:
As the best of chariot-warriors—many [princes] headed by Śatrughna—
and all the great kings with crores of chariots were proceeding,

suddenly on the path there arose a dreadful darkness,
in which neither one's own kin nor a stranger could be recognized by men and their relatives.

The sky was covered with dust, filled with lightning and thunder;
then, in such a terrifying turmoil,

clouds rained blood, pus, feces, and much else;
those warriors, who were foremost of adversaries, became exceedingly perturbed.

When the world was agitated, wondering 'What is this? What is this state?',
the eyes of men of renowned vigor were enveloped in darkness.

A friend of Rāvaṇa, dwelling in Pātāla,
renowned as Vidyunmālin, surrounded by ranks of rākṣasas, stole the horse.

Mounted on an aerial car that traveled at will and was made entirely of iron,
he indeed seized the horse, causing terror among the warriors.

In a moment that darkness vanished, and the sky shone clear;
those warriors headed by Śatrughna asked: "Where is that horse?"

All of them, looking at one another for the king of horses,
when they did not see the steed, an outcry of lamentation arose.

"Where is the horse of the horse sacrifice? By what wicked person has it been taken?"
While they were speaking thus, that lord of Danu's sons [and rākṣasas]

was seen by all the excellent soldiers mounted on chariots and shining with valour,
mounted on an excellent aerial car, surrounded by the foremost rākṣasas.

Evil-faced, with terrifying mouths, protruding fangs, dreadful,
the rākṣasas were seen there, eager to swallow the army.

Then they reported to Śatrughna, the foremost among the best of men:
"The horse has been taken by one sporting in an aerial chariot in the sky; we do not know [who it is].

"Having confounded us heroes with darkness, he approached
and seized the horse, O tiger among kings! Act as is fitting!"

Hearing their words, Śatrughna, filled with great fury, [said:]
"Who is this powerful rākṣasa who has seized my horse?

"Let that aerial chariot fall today, struck down by the mass of my arrows!
Let the head of that enemy of mine fall today beneath my razor-headed shafts!

"Let chariots be prepared by all, filled with great weapons and missiles!
Let the warriors march against him to slay the thief of the horse!"
Having spoken thus, his eyes red with anger, he addressed his minister, / who knew right policy from wrong, was valiant, and was skilled in matters of war:

Śatrughna said:
"O minister, tell me who should be dispatched, eager to kill the rākṣasa,
possessed of great weapons, exceedingly heroic, and best among those skilled in supreme missiles?

"Deliberate and tell me quickly; I will act according to your word.
Name the heroes suited for this, who are skilled in all missiles."

Hearing this, the minister spoke fitting words,
pointing out the heroes fit for the great battle, who swiftly bowed [before him].

Sumati said:
"Let Puṣkala go to conquer that rākṣasa, intent on victory in battle,
equipped with great weapons and missiles, a scorcher of his foes!

"Likewise, let Lakṣmīnidhi go, accompanied by a host of weapons;
let him shatter his vehicle with his sharp arrows!

"Hanūmān, daring in action, is capable of fighting the rākṣasas here;
let him strike the rākṣasas with his mouth and tail, O lord!

"And whichever monkey heroes are skilled in the art of battle,
let them all go to fight, urged on by your word!

"Sumada, Subāhu, and Pratāpāgrya, excellent men,
let them go to fight those vile rākṣasas with sharp arrows!

"You too, surrounded by great weapons and standing upon a chariot,
secure victory in battle, intent on slaying the rākṣasa!

"This is my opinion, O king: let those warriors who crush foes
go into battle, the heroic ones; what need of many other troops?"
When the foremost of heroes, the minister named Sumati, had spoken thus, / Śatrughna addressed the heroes skilled in battle.

"O heroes, Puṣkala and the rest, who are skilled in all weapons and missiles,
make your vows before me for the destruction of the rākṣasa!

"Having made a solemn vow, shining with your own prowess,
go into the midst of battle, full of might!"
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, those mighty warriors, / endowed with fiery energy, made their respective great vows.

Thereupon, first the heroic Puṣkala, hearing the king's words,
filled with supreme enthusiasm, uttered this vow.

Puṣkala said:
"Hear, O tiger among kings, my vow made through prowess,
exceedingly wondrous, while all the people listen!

"If I do not make the daitya fall into a swoon with sharp razor-headed shafts
shot from my bow, his face disordered with scattered hair,

"then whatever sin belongs to an enjoyer of [another's] maiden, whatever sin belongs to blasphemy of the gods,
may that sin indeed be mine if I make my word untrue!

"If the exceedingly mighty soldiers, pierced by my arrows,
do not fall, O great king, then hear my vow in that regard:

"Whoever makes a distinction between Viṣṇu and Īśa, or between Śiva and Śakti,
may that sin indeed be mine if I do not make my word true!

"All that has been spoken as my word: the unwavering devotion
that I have to the lotus feet of the lord of the Raghus will make it come true."

Hearing that vow of Puṣkala, king Lakṣmīnidhi
made a true vow, adorned with his own prowess.

Lakṣmīnidhi said:
"A man who, having heard abuse of the Vedas, sits like a mute,
and one who takes delight in his mind, excluded from all dharma,

"a brāhmaṇa of wicked conduct who sells liquids, lac, and the like,
and the fool who, deluded by greed for wealth, sells a cow,

"and he who drinks water from a mleccha's well and does not perform an expiation—
may that sin indeed be mine if I turn back!"
Then Hanūmān, skilled in battle, hearing his vow, / remembered the feet of Rāma and spoke auspicious words:
“My master is ever to be meditated upon in the heart by yogins again and again, / whom all the gods together with the Asuras revere with crest-jewels.
Rāma, glorious lord of Ayodhyā, worshipped by the lords of the worlds— / having remembered him, whatever word I speak, that shall indeed become true.
O king, who is this insignificant Daitya, weak, mounted on a flying chariot? / Speak quickly! I must strike him down all by myself.
I can weigh Mount Meru along with Indra on the tip of my tail; / I can dry up the entire ocean or drink up the cosmic fire.
By the grace of the king, the glorious lord of the Raghus, and of Jānakī, / there is nothing on the surface of the earth, O king, that could ever be impossible for me.
If this word spoken by me should be false, O lord, / then may I be excluded from devotion to the lord of the Raghus!
Whatever sin belongs to a Śūdra who keeps a brown cow for the sake of milk, / let that very sin be mine if I speak an untrue word!
Whatever sin belongs to a Śūdra who, overcome by lust, goes to a Brahmin woman out of infatuation, / let that very sin be mine if I speak an untrue word!
He who, greedy for the taste on his tongue, drinks that wine, / by smelling which one goes to hell and by touching which one goes to Raurava—
whatever sin arises for him, let that certainly be mine, / if, by the power of Rāma’s grace, I do not make what I vowed come true!”
When this was spoken by the great heroes, the warriors, filled with swiftness, / made a great vow displaying their own prowess.
Śatrughna also made a vow there before the eyes of the men, / applauding those warriors skilled in battle: “Well done! Well done!”
“I declare before you my own vow adorned with courage; / let the fortunate ones endowed with zeal for battle listen to it:
If I do not strike his head and fell it with arrows, / severed from his flying chariot and headless trunk onto the ground,
then whatever sin is incurred by false witness, whatever sin by the theft of gold, / whatever sin by reviling Brahmā—let that definitely be mine today!”
Having heard these good words of Śatrughna, those honored heroes [said]: / "Blessed are you, O brother of Rāghava! Who else could be superior to you?"
Indeed, by you was slain the Daitya who brought sorrow to gods and Dānavas, / named Lavaṇa, lord of the world, son of Madhu, possessed of great strength.
Who is this wicked Rākṣasa, and what is his insignificant strength? / In an instant, O high-minded one, you will bring about his destruction!”
Having spoken thus, those great heroes, prepared upon the battlefield, / marched joyfully against the rākṣasa in order to make their vow come true.

5.34.m: Śeṣa said: / In chariots yoked with noble steeds, full of splendor, laden with all weapons and missiles, / accompanied by various gems, they advanced against that vile Rākṣasa.
Seeing them, the Rākṣasa, standing in his flying chariot, spoke / in a voice deep as a thundercloud, as if repeatedly terrifying them:
“Let the warriors not fight; let them go back to their own dwelling! / Let them not abandon their lives; I will not release this excellent horse.
I am known as Vidyunmālin, a dear friend of Rāvaṇa; / I have come to make retribution on behalf of my departed friend.
Where is that Rāma who departed after striking down my friend Rāvaṇa? / And where is his brother, the crest-jewel of all warriors?
Having slain him, the younger brother of Rāma, I will obtain retribution for him, / drinking the blood rising with bubbles from the passage of his throat!”
Having heard these words, Puṣkala, the foremost and best among warriors, / addressed him who was endowed with valor and prowess.
Puṣkala said: / “Warriors do not utter boasts in battle; / they demonstrate their prowess through showers of their own weapons and missiles.
Having seized the horse of him by whom Rāvaṇa was slain / along with his friends and kin, where will you go, O arrogant fool?
You will fall by the arrows released from the bow of Śatrughna; / jackals will eat you as you lie fallen on the ground, bereft of life.
Do not roar, O wicked one, while I, the servant of Rāma, am present! / Warriors roar in battle after conquering the enemy, because of their great triumph!”
Śeṣa said: / As that heroic Puṣkala, wild in battle, was speaking thus, / the foremost Rākṣasa struck him forcefully in the heart with a javelin.
As that great iron javelin mounted with gold came flying, / that Puṣkala cut it down with three very fierce, sharp arrows.
Deprived of its brilliance by the arrows, it fell to the earth in three pieces; / as it fell, it shone like the threefold power of Viṣṇu.
Seeing that spear broken, the tormentor of foes, the Rākṣasa, / swiftly seized a three-pronged trident made of iron.
The lord of Rākṣasas hurled it, sharp-pointed and blazing like fire; / as it came, he named Puṣkala reduced it to sesame-sized pieces with arrows.
Having swiftly shattered the trident, that servant of Rāghava, / Puṣkala, took up his bow and sharp arrows swift as thought.
Those arrows struck swiftly into his heart, making it red with blood, / just as the captivating virtues of Viṣṇu produce devotion in the heart of a Vaiṣṇava.
Tormented by the pain of the piercing of those arrows, the haughty Vidyunmālin / seized a terrible club, intent on killing Puṣkala.
The club hurled by him named Vidyunmālin / struck [Puṣkala] in the heart, quickly bringing about fainting.
Struck by the club, shaking and trembling, that hero / Puṣkala, the tormentor of foes, fell onto the seat of his chariot.
Then his brother Ugradaṃṣṭra fought Lakṣmīnidhi / with various weapons and missiles discharged, which take away the lives of heroes.
Instantly regaining consciousness, Puṣkala said to the Rākṣasa: / “Blessed are you, foremost of Rākṣasas; your prowess is supreme!
Now look at my own great vow, honored by heroes: / today I will cast you down to the ground from your chariot with sharp arrows!”
Having spoken thus, he seized a sharp and irresistible arrow, / blazing with the fiery energy of fire and endowed with great nobility.
As soon as [the Rākṣasa] showed his prowess to counter it, / that very fierce arrow with a sharp point penetrated his heart.
Perplexed by that arrow, his mind reeling, that Rākṣasa / fell from the seat of his flying chariot to the ground, bereft of consciousness.
His elder brother was seen falling by Ugradaṃṣṭra; / grasping him, fearing the enemy, he brought him inside the chariot.
In great rage, he spoke to the enemy, Puṣkala, the foremost among the strong: / “Having struck down my brother, where will you go, O wicked-minded one?
Only by utterly conquering me in battle will you attain supreme victory; / while I remain, let the hope of victory be turned away from your heart!”
While he was speaking thus, [Puṣkala], his eyes filled with wrath, / swiftly struck that wicked one in the heart with ten arrows.
Struck with ten arrows by the high-souled Puṣkala, / the evil-minded one grew enraged in his heart and set out to slay him.

Grinding his teeth in anger, he raised his fist and struck,
roaring loudly, creating in [every] heart the fear of a thunderbolt strike.

Struck by the fist, the hero Puṣkala, skilled in supreme missiles,
did not tremble, desiring the crushing of that wicked-souled one.

He unleashed sharp calf-tooth-tipped arrows into [the demon's] chest;
pained by those arrows, the daitya seized a trident.

Blazing, three-pronged, exceedingly terrifying with garlands of flames,
that dreadful [trident] struck the chest of the great hero Puṣkala.

Struck by that trident, the best of archers swooned;
having fallen into a deep faint, he collapsed onto his chariot.

Knowing that he had fallen into a swoon, Hanūmān, the son of the wind god,
his heart agitated with fury, spoke to that rākṣasa:

"Where are you going, evil-minded one, while I remain as a fighter?
I will kill you with kicks of my feet—you who have come as the thief of the horse!"

Having spoken thus, standing in the sky, he tore with the tips of his claws
and killed the great daityas, the enemy soldiers standing in the aerial chariot.

Some were struck with his tail, some struck with the soles of his feet,
and some were torn apart with both arms by the son of the wind.

Some were destroyed and killed, some were struck down in a faint,
and others fled, afflicted by the terror of the blows of his feet.

Many exceedingly dreadful rākṣasas were killed there;
they were cut down, torn asunder, and split into two by the son of the wind.

That aerial chariot which moved at will, its walls and archways broken,
was surrounded on all sides by asuras crying out in despair.

As Hanūmān fought heroically, now on the ground, now in the sky,
that vehicle moving at will, difficult to approach, could be seen here and there.

Wherever that aerial chariot went, right there the monkey born of the wind,
assuming forms at will, was seen striking.

When the great multitude standing in the aerial chariot was thus thrown into confusion,
the daitya lord Ugradaṃṣṭra approached Hanūmān.

"O monkey, you have performed a great feat in striking down the warriors!
If you stand for a moment, I shall sever your life!"

Having spoken thus, that evil-minded one struck Hanūmān
with a very sharp trident shining with the brilliance of blazing fire.

The mighty one caught in his mouth that incoming trident
and crushed it entirely, though forged completely of iron.

Having crushed that iron trident discharged by the daitya,
the powerful Hanumān struck him with many slaps of his hand.

Struck by the lord of monkeys with slaps here and there,
he, in agony, unleashed an illusion that caused terror to all the worlds.

Then an intense darkness arose in which no one at all could be seen,
wherein many people did not recognize their own kin from strangers.

Rocks resembling mountain peaks fell upon the good warriors;
struck by them, they all became bewildered.
Lightnings flashed there, dense rain clouds roared, / they rained pus and blood, and released filthy water.
And many headless trunks were seen falling from the sky, / with severed heads adorned with earrings.
Naked, exceedingly deformed, with disheveled hair, and terrible faces, / dreadful Daityas causing terror were seen on every side.
Then the people, agitated and terrified of one another, / took to flight, considering it a great portent of disaster.
Then the highly renowned Śatrughna arrived standing in his chariot; / remembering Śrī Rāma, he placed arrows upon his bow.
Having dispersed that illusion with the Mohanāstra weapon, the valiant one, / scattering showers of arrows in the sky, rained them down upon the demon in battle.
Then the directions became clear, and the sun shone bright; / the clouds dispersed the way they came, and the lightnings subsided.
Then a flying chariot filled with Rākṣasas was seen ahead, / exceedingly large and turbulent with shouts of "Cut! Pierce!"
Hundreds of thousands of arrows adorned with golden fletchings / repeatedly fell upon the flying chariot moving at will in the sky.
Then the flying chariot was broken and was no longer seen on high; / it lay on the ground in one place like a shattered piece of its own city.
Then the enraged Daitya fitted arrows to his bow; / scattering Rāma's brother with those arrows, he roared.
Hundreds of those sharp-pointed arrows struck his body in abundance; / they looked splendid, carrying streams of blood.
Endowed with supreme power, Śatrughna placed upon his bow / the Vāyavya weapon whose deity is Vāyu, which caused the Rākṣasas to tremble.
Struck by that weapon, demons falling from the sky with disheveled hair / were seen like swarms of sky-faring bhūtas and vetālas.
Seeing that weapon discharged by Raghunātha's brother, / the son of Danu fitted the Pāśupata weapon onto his bow.
Thereupon vetālas, bhūtas, pretas, and night-roving demons surged forward, / bearing skulls and shears, drinking abundant blood.
Indeed, they joyfully drank the blood of Śatrughna's heroes, / even of the living, irresistible and resplendent with shears in hand.
Seeing that weapon pervading all, crushing the warriors, / he discharged the weapon named Nārāyaṇāstra to repel it.
The Nārāyaṇāstra immediately warded off all of them; / urged on by the night-roamer, they all met their destruction.
Then the enraged night-roamer Vidyunmālin seized / a fierce, sharp, and dreadful trident to kill Śatrughna.
As Vidyunmālin approached in battle with the trident in his hand, / [Śatrughna] struck his arm with crescent-tipped arrows.
His arm severed by those arrows, he rushed forward to strike with his head: / "You are slain! Begone, Śatrughna! Who will be your protector?"
As he was speaking thus, with sharp arrows he swiftly severed / the head, adorned with earrings, of that strong and heroic [warrior].
Seeing him decapitated, the powerful Ugradaṃṣṭra / began to strike with his fist Śatrughna, who was attended by heroes.
Śatrughna, however, with a razor-sharp arrow cut off the head / of the warriors skilled in all weapons who were rushing onto the battlefield.
The surviving Rākṣasas, now left leaderless, all fled; / then, bowing before Śatrughna, they surrendered the captured horse.
Then the sounds of vīṇās and the blasts of conches on every side, / and the charming victory shouts of the valiant warriors, were heard.

5.35.m: Śeṣa said: / Having recovered that horse captured by the Rākṣasas, King Śatrughna, / accompanied by Puṣkala, experienced immense joy.
Those warriors, their limbs sprinkled with blood, along with Lakṣmīnidhi, / praised the great king who was filled with enthusiasm for battle.
When that great, unconquerable Daitya Vidyunmālin was slain, / all the gods cast away their fear and attained great happiness, O sage.
The rivers became clear, and the sun became bright; / breezes blew, sprinkled with fragrant water and possessing pure vigor.
Those great heroes, clad in armor, standing in chariots, with clean bodies, / and endowed with the glory of victory, all said to the king:
The heroes said: / By good fortune, O highly wise one, the Daitya Vidyunmālin has been slain by you, / out of fear of whom the gods were terrified and driven from heaven.
By good fortune the splendid, great horse of Raghunātha has been regained; / by good fortune you shall march everywhere and conquer the circle of the earth.
O lord, release this steed, charming and swift as thought; / let there be no delay in time here, O highly wise one.
Śeṣa said: / Having heard those timely words of the heroes, / praising them with "Well done! Well done!", he released the excellent horse.
Released, it roamed toward the northern region, well-protected / by the best charioteers, infantrymen, and horses, skilled in all weapons and missiles.
Listen, O Vātsyāyana, to this captivating account of what happened there to Śatrughna, / which burns away heaps of sins.
He then reached the bank of the Revā, served by hosts of sages, / which was like the essence of a heap of blue sapphires under the guise of water.
Bowing to all those best sages, surrounded by warriors, / he followed behind the gem of a horse that roamed wherever it pleased.
While proceeding, [he saw] there an aged hermitage built of palāśa leaves, / sprinkled by the billowing waves of the Revā, an abode that removes sin.
Seeing it, Śatrughna, skilled in all duties regarding dharma and practical affairs, / spoke to Sumati, who was omniscient and versed in policy:
The king said: / O minister, tell me, whose sacred-looking hermitage is this? / O best among those skilled in inquiry, tell this to me who am asking.
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these words, Sumati spoke to the king / in clear, smiling speech, showing his own affection:
Sumati said: / By seeing him, O great king, we shall indeed become cleansed of sin, / [seeing] that best of sages devoted to all sacred scriptures.
Therefore, having bowed, inquire of him; he will tell you everything; / he is exceedingly eager for the nectar of Raghunātha's lotus feet.
Known by the name Āraṇyaka, a worshipper of Raghunātha's feet, / he is filled with exceedingly severe asceticism and skilled in the meaning of all sacred treatises.
Having heard those words of his, reinforced with dharma and worldly welfare, / he then set out, accompanied by a few attendants, to see him.
Hanumān, the heroic Puṣkala, Sumati the best of ministers, / Lakṣmīnidhi of foremost majesty, Subāhu, and Sumada—
Surrounded by these, the noble-minded King Śatrughna arrived at the hermitage / to pay homage to Āraṇyaka, the best of the twice-born.
Having approached, he then offered obeisance to that best of ascetics, / together with all those heroes whose necks were bent in modesty.
Seeing all those kings, headed by Śatrughna, bowed low, / he then offered water for hospitality and foot-washing, along with fruits and roots.
He said to all those kings: "Where have you met together? / How have you come here? Tell all of that, O sinless ones."
Hearing these words of that best of sages, O brāhmaṇa, / Sumati, skilled in disputation, spoke:
Sumati said: / "This horse of the king of Raghu's lineage is guarded by all; / the hero will perform a sacrifice supplied with every requisite."
Hearing that statement of theirs, the best of sages spoke, / as if dispelling all terrible darkness with the radiance of his teeth:
The forest-dweller said: / "What use are diverse other sacrifices supplied with every requisite, / which certainly yield meager merit and grant a perishable status?
A deluded person, abandoning Hari, worships another— / [Hari,] the hero of the Raghus, the lord of Ramā, who bestows a state of enduring sovereignty.
He who, merely remembered by men, carries away a mountain of sins— / abandoning him, a fool torments himself with sacrifices, yogas, vows, and the like.
Ah, behold the delusion of people, how exceedingly deceived they are! / Leaving aside the worship of Rāma, which is easy to attain, one practices what is hard to attain.
He is contemplated by those with desires or even by yogins free from desires; / he grants liberation to men, destroying all sins merely when remembered.
Formerly, in my search for reality, seeking out a wise man, / I went to many holy sites, but no one pointed out the truth to me.
Then, through great fortune indeed, the sage Lomaśa was encountered— / arrived from heaven with the desire of making a pilgrimage.
Then, bowing down to that great sage, I questioned him— / that long-lived one, whose two feet are served by great yogins:
"O master, today a wondrous and hard-to-attain human birth has been obtained by me; / wishing to cross over the terrible ocean of cyclic existence, what should be done?
Deliberate and tell: Is that a vow, a gift, a muttered prayer, a sacrifice, / or a god who indeed conveys one across the ocean of cyclic existence?
Knowing which, from the ocean of your mercy, I may cross this terrible cyclic existence— / tell me that, O lord of yoga, you who have crossed to the other side of all scriptures' meaning."
Having heard these words of mine, the best of sages said: / "Listen with a single-pointed mind, O brāhmaṇa, endowed with supreme faith!"
There are gifts, holy sites, vows, restraints, observances, / and yogas, and likewise many sacrifices; they are bestowers of heaven.
I shall proclaim the supreme secret, the destroyer of all sins; / hear that, O highly fortunate one, which conveys one across the ocean of cyclic existence.
It must not be told to an atheist, nor again to one without faith; / it must not be given to a slanderer, a rogue, nor an enemy of devotion.
It should be told to a devotee of Rāma, peaceful, free from desire and wrath— / this supreme [secret] that causes the destruction of all suffering.
There is no god higher than Rāma; there is no vow higher than Rāma; / there is no yoga higher than Rāma; there is no sacrifice higher than Rāma.
Remembering him, murmuring his name, and worshipping him supreme, a man / attains the highest prosperity, both in this world and the next.
Recalled and meditated upon with the mind, he grants the fruits of all desires; / he gives supreme devotion, which conveys one across the ocean of cyclic existence.
Even an outcaste, having remembered Rāma, attains the supreme destination; / what then of those like you, devoted to the Vedas and scriptures?
The secret of all the Vedas and scriptures has been revealed to you; / act accordingly, so that your desire may be fulfilled.
There is one god: Rāmacandra; there is one vow: his worship; / there is one mantra: his name; and scripture is indeed his praise.
Therefore, worship delightful Rāmacandra with all your being, / so that the ocean of cyclic existence becomes trifling like a cow's hoofprint."
[The forest-dweller said:] "Having heard those words of his, I made another inquiry: / 'How is the god meditated upon, or how is he worshipped by men?
Tell me in full, O all-knowing one of great intellect, / knowing which I may achieve my goal in the three worlds, O best of sages.'"
