[The forest-dweller said:] "Having heard this speech of mine and having reflected, that Lomaśa / told me everything, beginning with meditation on Rāma:
[Lomaśa said:] "Listen, O best of brāhmaṇas; I shall tell what was asked by you, O sinless one, / how the lord of Ramā, the burner of the fever of cyclic existence, is pleased.
In the delightful city of Ayodhyā, adorned with splendid pavilions, / at the base of the wish-fulfilling tree that grants the fulfillment of all desires, one should meditate
upon a throne adorned with great emeralds, gold, sapphires, and other gems, / captivating to the mind, dispelling darkness by its radiance.
Seated upon it, the delightful king of the Raghus, / his body dark as a blade of dūrvā grass, worshipped by the lord of the gods,
possessing a face that scorns the beauty of the full moon of the full-moon night, / bearing a forehead resembling the crescent of the eighth-day moon,
abounding in the beauty of black locks, adorned with a jewel-crested crown, / radiant with beautiful earrings shaped like makaras,
shining with lips having the fine luster of coral, / beautifully adorned with rows of teeth shaped like the rays of the moon,
his face adorned with a sweet tongue like a china-rose, / upon which dwell the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, along with the scriptures,
adorned with the beauty of a neck possessing the luster of a conch shell, / bearing broad, fleshy, noble shoulders like a lion,
bearing arms with long limbs, marked with armlets and bracelets, / adorned with the splendors of rings and diamonds, reaching down to the knees,
bearing a broad chest adorned by the dwelling of Lakṣmī, / marked with the wondrous signs of Śrīvatsa and others, exceedingly captivating,
with a large belly, a deep navel, radiant with fine hips, / endowed especially with beauty by means of a jeweled girdle,
with two spotless thighs, splendid knees adorned with glory, / and two feet adorned with the auspicious lines of the thunderbolt, the barley-corn, and the goad,
which are to be meditated on by yogins, tender and radiant. / Having meditated on and remembered [him], you will cross the ocean of cyclic existence.
Always worshipping him with sandalwood paste and the like as one wishes, / one attains supreme prosperity, both in this world and the next.
The supreme meditation on Rāma was asked by you, O great king; / that has been told to you. Cross now the ocean of cyclic existence."

5.36.m: Śeṣa said: / Having heard this supreme, great [teaching] from Lomaśa, the chief of brāhmaṇas / again questioned that sage, all-knowing and best among yogins.
The forest-dweller said: / "O best of sages, tell me this; I ask you, O highly intelligent one! / Endowed with compassion, teachers speak everything to a servant.
Who is this Rāma, O highly fortunate one, who is constantly meditated on by you? / What are his deeds? Tell me, O bull among the twice-born!
For what purpose did he descend? Why did he take on human state? / Tell me all that swiftly, for the dispelling of my doubt."
Śeṣa said: / Having heard this exceedingly beautiful speech of the sage, / Lomaśa related the wondrous deeds of Rāma:
[Lomaśa said:] "Seeing the worlds plunged into hell, the lord of lords of yoga [descended] / in order to spread fame in the world, by which one will cross what is terrible.
Knowing this, the ocean of mercy, the captivating supreme Lord, / accompanied by Śrī, took an incarnation here in four forms.
Formerly, when the Tretā age arrived, the delight of the Raghus, with his complete portion, / the lotus-eyed Rāma was born in the solar dynasty."
That Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, wearing side-locks of hair, was a youth; / and by their father's command, the two were devoted to following Viśvāmitra.
The two boys were given by the king to protect the sacrifice; / self-controlled, bow-bearing heroes, devoted to following Viśvāmitra.
As the two were journeying along the path, an ogre named Tāṭakā / met them in the dreadful forest, indeed to cause an obstacle to them.
By the ṛṣi's command, Rāma, the Rāghava, dispatched Tāṭakā / to the torment of Yama by his mastery of the science of archery.
Ahalyā, Gautama's wife, who had been turned into a rock through the act of Indra, / by the touch of the sole of his foot was reborn in her true form.
When Viśvāmitra's sacrifice was well underway, the best of Raghus / struck down Mārīca and Subāhu with supreme arrows.
The bow of the Lord that stood in Janaka's palace was broken; / in his fifteenth year, Rāma [won] the princess of Mithilā, then six years old.
He wed in marriage the charming Sītā, who was not born of a womb; / having won Sītā, the Rāghava was then fulfilled in his aim.
Then for twelve years Rāma took delight with her; / in his twenty-seventh year, [the king] arranged his heir-apparency.
Then Kaikeyī begged two boons of the king; / by one of them: "Let Rāma, together with Sītā and accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa,
wearing matted hair, wander forth for fourteen years here; / and by the second, let Bharata be my master of heir-apparency!"
The king sent Rāma into exile together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; / for three nights he had only water as food, and on the fourth day ate fruit.
On the fifth day, Rāma made his dwelling on Citrakūṭa; / then in the thirteenth year, O great sage, at Pañcavaṭī,
Rāma disfigured Śūrpaṇakhā, the night-roaming ogre-woman; / and as he roamed the forest together with Jānakī,
the ogre came to abduct her as a consequence of sins; / then on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, in the hour named Vṛnda,
the ten-necked one abducted Sītā in the absence of the two descendants of Raghu. / As she was thus being carried off by him, she wailed like an osprey:
"Rāma, Rāma! Save me, save me who am carried off by an ogre!" / Just as a hawk overcome by hunger might carry off a crying quail,
so Rāvaṇa, overcome by lust, carried off Janaka's daughter. / As he was thus carrying off Janaka's daughter, Jaṭāyu, the king of birds, then
fought with the lord of ogres; and struck down by Rāvaṇa, he fell. / But on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, as she was living in Rāvaṇa's abode,
Sampāti told of her among the monkeys in the tenth month. / On the eleventh day, from Mount Mahendra, [Hanumān] leapt across a hundred leagues.
Hanumān searched through Laṅkā during that night; / at the end of that night, Hanumān indeed had the sight of Sītā.
On the twelfth day Hanumān took his station in a śiṃśapā tree; / in that night there was conversation to gain the confidence of Jānakī.
Then on the thirteenth day a battle took place with Akṣa and others; / and on the fourteenth day the monkey was bound with the weapon of Brahmā by the conqueror of Indra.
The burning of Laṅkā was accomplished by fire joined to his tail; / on the full-moon day the monkey returned to Mount Mahendra.
Five days were spent on the path from the first day of the dark fortnight of Mārga; / having returned, on the sixth day, the Honey Grove was indeed destroyed.
On the seventh day occurred the delivery of the token of recognition and the reporting of everything; / on the eighth, under the asterism Uttarā Phālgunī, at the hour named Vijaya,
when the thousand-rayed sun had reached the meridian, occurred the setting out of the Rāghava; / having made a vow, Rāma departed for the southern direction:
"Crossing even the ocean, I will slay the lord of ogres." / When he departed for the southern direction, Sugrīva also became his friend.
In seven days occurred the pitching of the camp by the ocean; / from the first day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa up to the third,
the arrival of the Rāghava with his army took place at the ocean; / and on the fourth day, Bibhīṣaṇa united with Rāma.
For crossing the ocean, he undertook deliberation on the fifth day; / Rāma undertook waiting for death without food for four days.
There was the obtaining of the boon from the ocean together with the indication of a means; / then on the tenth day was the commencement, and on the thirteenth the completion.
On the fourteenth day Rāma stationed his army on Mount Suvela; / from the full-moon day to the end of the second, the ferrying across of the army took three days.
Having crossed the ocean, Rāma, accompanied by the army of the lord of monkeys / and accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, besieged the city of Laṅkā for the sake of Sītā.
From the third to the end of the tenth day was the encampment, for eight days; / the arrival of Śuka and Sāraṇa took place there on the eleventh day.
On the twelfth day named the dark fortnight of Pauṣa occurred the counting of the army, / and the description by Śārdūla of the sudden assault of the monkey lords.
From the thirteenth to the new-moon day, in three days, in Laṅkā / Rāvaṇa then carried out the muster of the army and the rousing for battle.
Aṅgada went on the embassy on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha; / and then occurred Sītā's seeing of her husband's illusory head and other limbs.
From the second day of Māgha for seven days up to the eighth, / there was tumultuous battle between the ogres and the monkeys.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, at night, in battle by Indrajit, / the binding of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with the serpent-noose was indeed done.
When the monkey leaders were distraught and despondent on all sides, / to release the serpent-noose the Wind whispered on the tenth day
into the ear the true nature of Rāma; then came Garuḍa. / On the eleventh and twelfth days, the slaying of Dhūmrākṣa was accomplished.
On the thirteenth day, Kampana was slain in battle by that very [hero]; / from the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha to the first day of the dark fortnight,
in three days, the slaying of Prahasta was executed by Nīla; / from the second day of the dark fortnight of Māgha to the fourth, in three days,
Rāvaṇa was routed from the battle by Rāma in a tumultuous fight; / from the fifth day up to the eighth, [Kumbhakarṇa] was awakened by Rāvaṇa.
Kumbhakarṇa then feasted for four days; / Kumbhakarṇa, in six days from the ninth to the fourteenth,
the devourer of many monkeys, was slain in battle by Rāma; / on the new-moon day there was a cessation of hostilities out of grief.
From the first day of the beginning of Phālguna to the fourth, in four days, / five ogres, Bisatantu and others, were slain.
From the fifth to the seventh occurred the slaying of Atikāya; / from the eighth to the twelfth, over five days, were slain
Nikumbha and Kumbha, and after that Makarākṣa in three days; / on the day of the second of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, victory was won by the conqueror of Indra.
From the third to the end of the seventh, for five days, / there was a cessation of hostilities because of preoccupation with bringing the herbs.
Then, up to the thirteenth, in five days, Indrajit, / renowned for strength and manly valour, was slain in battle by Lakṣmaṇa.
On the fourteenth day the ten-necked one received consecration after the cessation; / on the new-moon day the ten-necked one went forth to battle.
From the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra to the fifth, in five days, / while Rāvaṇa was fighting, there was an abundant slaughter of ogres.
From the sixth of Caitra to the eighth occurred the slaying of Mahāpārśva and others; / on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the piercing of the son of Sumitrā by the spear [occurred].
The ten-necked one was put to flight by Rāma filled with wrath; / Mount Droṇa was brought by the son of Añjanā for the sake of Lakṣmaṇa.
On the tenth [day] there was a withdrawal in the night battle of the demons; / but on the eleventh, Mātali the charioteer,
sent by Indra, offered a chariot to Rāma with devotion in the battle. / Then, enraged, from the twelfth up to the dark fourteenth,
in eighteen days, Rāma slew Rāvaṇa in single combat. / When the fierce battle took place, Rāma attained victory.
From the bright second of Māgha to the dark fourteenth of Caitra, / thus among the eighty-seven days, an interval of fifteen days
was the battle's cessation, [and] the combat lasted seventy-two days. / The funeral rites of Rāvaṇa and the others took place on the new moon day.
On the first lunar day of Vaiśākha, Rāma dwelt upon the battlefields. / On the second, Vibhīṣaṇa was consecrated to the kingdom of Laṅkā.
On the third was Sītā's purification and the receiving of boons from the gods. / Having finally slain the lord of Laṅkā, he, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa,
took the holy Jānakī, who had been grieved by the demon; / taking Jānakī with supreme love, he returned.
On the fourth of Vaiśākha, Rāma mounted the Puṣpaka [chariot]; / he returned through the sky once again toward the city of Ayodhyā.
When the fourteenth year was complete, on the fifth of Mādhava, / Rāma, along with his retinue, arrived at the hermitage of Bharadvāja.
On the sixth he met with Bharata at Nandigrāma; / on the seventh he, the scion of Raghu, was consecrated in Ayodhyā.
For eleven months and fourteen days, / the princess of Mithilā lived separated from Rāma in Rāvaṇa's abode.
In his forty-second year, Rāma ruled the kingdom; / and Sītā was thirty-three years [old] then.
At the end of the fourteen years, entering the city, / the lord Rāma, joyful, having slain Rāvaṇa in battle,
then ruled the kingdom there together with his brothers. / As he was ruling the kingdom, his family priest, the best of speakers,
Agastya, the jar-born, will come to that lord of Raghu. / At his word, this lord of Raghu will perform a horse sacrifice.
His horse will indeed come to your hermitage, O you of noble vows; / his warriors, full of joy, will come to your hermitage.
Before them you will recite the delightful tales of Rāma; / together with them you will go to Ayodhyā, O best of the twice-born.
Beholding Rāma in Ayodhyā, whose eyes resemble lotus petals, / instantly cross beyond the ocean of worldly existence.’
Having spoken thus to me, the best of sages, Lomaśa, who was wise in all matters, / said: "What is to be asked by you?" Then I spoke what was beneficial.
‘By your grace, all the wondrous deeds of Rāma are known; / by your favor, I shall reach the lotus feet of Rāma.’
Bowed to by me, that lord of sages then departed; / by his favor, the worship of Rāma's feet was attained by me.
That very I remember the feet of Rāma daily and repeatedly; / I sing of his life constantly, untiring.
I purify other people with song that captivates the mind; / I rejoice, remembering again and again the sage’s word with the longing to see him.
Blessed am I! Accomplished in my purpose am I! Fortunate am I on the earth’s surface! / The desire to see the lotus feet of Rāmacandra will be mine.
Therefore, with all one's heart, the enchanting Rāma is to be worshipped; / indeed, he is to be revered by all who wish to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
Therefore, for what purpose have you all arrived? Or which king of men, / virtuous in nature, is performing the great sacrificial rite, the horse sacrifice?
Let all of that be told here by you who go to guard the horse; / may they remember the foot of the lord of Raghu, recalling it again and again!”
Having heard these words of the sage, struck with wonder, / remembering the lord of the Raghus, they addressed the sage Āraṇyaka:

5.37.m: Śeṣa said: / Questioned by the best of sages concerning the wondrous deeds of Rāma, / considering themselves blessed and fortunate, they spoke with respect.
The people said: / “We all are now purified by your sight, / since you purify us people now with the story of Rāma.
Listen to our true word; you are the best of brahmin seers. / Whatever you have asked of us, we shall tell it all.
At Agastya's word, for the removal of the sin of slaying a brahmin, the glorious, / great Rāma is performing a sacrifice, equipped with all provisions.
Protecting that [horse], all of us have indeed arrived at your hermitage / together with the horse, O brahmin; know this, O noble-minded one!”
Having heard these words, which were an enchanting elixir, / the brāhmaṇa, devoted to Rāma, attained supreme joy.
“Today the tree of my desire, endowed with beauty, has borne fruit; / today my mother is blessed, who gave birth to me who am born.
Today a kingdom free from thorns has been attained by me; / today the treasuries are fully prosperous; today the gods are well satisfied.
The fruit of the agnihotra, offered with clarified butter, has been attained by me today, / since I shall behold the two lotus feet of Rāmacandra.
The lord, ruler of Ayodhyā, who is constantly meditated upon in the heart, / that charming one will surely come within the range of my sight.
Embracing me, Hanūmat will ask of my welfare; / seeing my great devotion, that best of beings will attain satisfaction!”
Having heard these words, Hanūmān, the best of monkeys, / seized indeed the pair of feet of the sage Āraṇyaka.
“O master, O brahmin seer! I, Hanūmat, your servant, stand before you; / know me, O lord of sages, as akin to a grain of dust to the servant of Rāma!”
When he had spoken thus, the sage, exceedingly delighted, / embraced Hanūmān, who shone brilliantly with devotion to Rāma.
Both overcome with love, both drenched with nectar, / they stood motionless there as if painted in a picture.
Seated there, their minds filled with love for the lotus feet of the lord of Raghu, / they exchanged most delightful stories.
Hanūmat addressed these words of manifold beauty / to the forest hermit, the best of sages, engrossed in meditating on Rāma's feet:
“O master, this great diamond-sprout of Daśaratha's lineage, / Rāma's brother, the mighty hero Śatrughna, bows to you.
By him was slain Lavaṇa, the terrifier of all the worlds, / and all the sages, rich in asceticism, were made happy.
This one named Puṣkala bows to you, served by eminent warriors, / by whom great champions have now been conquered on the battleground.
Know this highly virtuous, mighty minister of Rāma, / dear as life to the lord of Raghu, omniscient, skilled in dharma.
This Subāhu is extremely fierce, a forest fire to the lineage of his enemies; / a bee at the lotus of Rāma's feet, of great fame, he bows to you.
And this Sumada, granted by Pārvatī through service to Rāma's feet, / has now attained a great crossing of the ocean of worldly existence.
This Satyavān, who, hearing from a servant that the horse had arrived, / offered up his kingdom, bows down to you on the earth.”
Having heard these words, having embraced him with deep respect, / the sage Āraṇyaka extended a welcome with fruits and other offerings.
Delighted, they spent the night there in the hermitage of the best of sages. / In the morning, having performed their daily rites in the Revā, those greatly energetic men,
Placing the sage together with his attendants upon a litter, / Śatrughna brought [him] to Ayodhyā, where Rāma had made his abode.
Seeing from afar the city inhabited by the kings of the solar dynasty, / he swiftly proceeded on foot out of a desire to see Raghunātha.
Having reached the delightful city of Ayodhyā, adorned with people, / he mounted upon thousands of longings to behold Rāma.
There, on the bank of the Sarayū in an adorned pavilion, / he saw Rāma, dark as a blade of dūrvā grass, with eyes possessing the splendor of a lotus,
Bearing an attractive deer horn at his waist, endowed with royal majesty, / surrounded by hosts of sages headed by Vyāsa, well-served by heroic warriors,
Surrounded by Bharata and Sumitrā's son [Lakṣmaṇa], / distributing gifts requested by the poor and the blind.
Beholding him, this one named Āraṇyaka considered himself fulfilled: / “My eyes, resembling lotus petals, behold Rāma!
Today my knowledge of all the treatises has become immensely fruitful, / since having learned of Śrī Rāma, I have reached this city of Ayodhyā!”

Having spoken many such words, rejoicing, / his body radiant with great delight at the sight of Rāma's feet, / he departed for the presence of the Lord of Ramā, inaccessible to others, / far beyond even the masters of yoga devoted to reflection.
Saying, “Blessed am I today! I shall bring Rāma’s feet into the range of my vision,” / speaking charming words, he looked upon Rāma.
Rāma also, seeing the best of Brahmins blazing with his own splendor, / an embodiment of asceticism, then rose up to greet him.
The great Rāmacandra bowed down for a long time at his feet: / “O deity devoted to Brahmins, today my body has been sanctified!”
As he was uttering these words, the lord fell at his feet, / his feet illuminated by the crest-jewels of gods and asuras bowing down.
Lifting that best of kings who bowed down, the great ascetic, chief among Brahmins, / embraced the beloved Lord in his arms.
The son of Kausalyā placed him on a lofty jewel-studded seat, / and the Lord washed both his feet with water.
Hari himself placed that foot-washing water upon his head, / saying, “Today I, along with my retinue and family, am purified.”
Having anointed him with sandalwood paste, he gave [him] a milch cow, / and he who is served by the lord of gods spoke charming words:
“Master, the sacrifice named the horse sacrifice is being performed by me; / through the arrival of your feet, today it will become complete.
Today, purified by your feet, / the horse sacrifice will effect the destruction of my sin born of killing a Brahmin.”
To him who was uttering these words, served by kings and emperors, / the sage Āraṇyaka, smiling, said this in a voice as sweet as mead:
“O master, ruler of the earth who honors Brahmins, your words are indeed fitting; / Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas are your forms, O great king.
When you perform auspicious deeds such as the worship of Brahmins, / then all kings will worship the Brahmin, O king.
As for what you said, O great king, ‘I perform a spotless sacrifice to dispel the killing of a Brahmin’— / that indeed is laughable speech!
From remembering your name, a fool destitute of all learning in the treatises, / crossing over the ocean of all sins, would go to the supreme abode.
This is clearly the essential meaning of all the Vedas and legendary histories: / that the remembrance of Rāma’s name is practiced as the deliverer from sin.
Sins, even those equal to killing a Brahmin, roar only so long / as your name, O Rāmacandra, is not clearly uttered.
Hearing the roar of your name, the elephants of great sins / flee anywhere, O great king, seeking a place of refuge.
Therefore, how could there be the sin of killing for you, the sight of whom yields great merit? / O Rāma, hearing your auspicious story, one becomes instantly purified.
Formerly in the Kṛta age, I heard this statement / from the mouth of sages dwelling on the bank of the Gaṅgā who knew antiquity:
‘Fears of sin exist for timorous, deeply sinful men only so long / as one does not speak with one's voice the charming name of Rāma.’”
"Therefore, fortunate am I today; the destruction of my cycle of rebirth / has now become easy to attain, O Rāmacandra, from the sight of you."
When he had spoken thus, all the sages there worshipped that sage, / saying, "Excellent, excellent are these words!"
Śeṣa said: / There a great wonder occurred; hear that from me as I tell it, / O Vātsyāyana, best of sages, devoted to devotion to Rāma.
Seeing the great king Rāma, such as he appears within the scope of meditation, / he experienced extreme joy and addressed the lords of sages:
“O lords of sages, hear my very charming statement! / Who in the world of mortals could ever be as fortunate as I?
There is no one equal to me, none has been born, nor will there ever be, / since Rāmabhadra, having bowed to me, inquired after my well-being!
He the dust of whose lotus feet is ever sought by the Vedas, / today drinking the water from my feet, considered himself purified!”
As he was speaking thus, a bursting forth from the Brahma-aperture took place; / the splendor arising from it came forth and entered into the leader of the Raghus.
As all the people looked on in the pavilion on the bank of the Sarayū, / he attained the liberation of union [with the Lord], difficult to obtain even by yogins.
In heaven there was the sound of horns, and then the sound of vīṇās; / a shower of flowers fell before them, a wonderful and marvelous sight for those looking on.
The sages too, seeing this, praised the lord of sages: / “Fulfilled is this best of sages, since Rāma’s body was beheld by him!”
